limbs.label: New: not raised and decided in 1987

rubric.mapping: Each limb comes from the reopen research score 0-5 on the same limb, times 10 (0=nothing, 1=inference or gap, 2=several documented facts, 3=a primary official record shows the anomaly, 4=a primary document proves the limb, 5=admissible originals ready for counsel). Total = sum of the four limbs, 0-200.
rubric.threshold_note: 100 = the Takhar threshold plausibly met; 200 = proved beyond doubt on every limb. Ready for counsel needs at least 40 on every limb.
rubric.order: Score high to low; ties by limb 2 (operative cause), then limb 3.
rubric.limb3_note: Takhar v Gracefield Developments Ltd [2019] UKSC 13: a party who shows a judgment was obtained by deception need not show it could not have been found with reasonable diligence at the time; the position differs where the point was raised and decided at trial. Limb 3 measures that.

source.note: Rows with a reopen_ground id take their four limbs from our reopen research (each 0-5 limb score x10). Rows with seed_score true were scored when Mr Wolf was built (1 Nov 2026) and wait for their first reopen-research test.

quarantine_note: Kissed-frog items are quarantined, under scrutiny, and never scored here.

rows.title: She never accepted permission: 1949–1974 refusals and her reply to the licence letters
rows.what: The 1987 decision turned on one finding: that Mary (Nancy) Williams never told BP she rejected the 31 October 1974 licence letters. The judgment's own account shows she had no real chance to. The letters were sent to her solicitor, who received them on the morning of 4 November; the judge stayed execution pending her agreement; and BP withdrew the warrant before she had given her solicitor any instructions. In the court's words, BP 'neither sought nor waited for her acceptance'. Every earlier attempt to make her occupation permissive had been refused, she was pleading ownership in an action never heard, and the family record is that she wrote back.

why.a: None held yet. Rises when her reply, or BP's 1984–86 list of documents, shows a rejection the court was told did not exist.
why.b: This is the reason BP won: the court wrote that 'it may be that the result would have been different' had she plainly rejected the letters.
why.c: The 4 November timing is in the judgment, so it was before the court; her reply, the full refusal chain (1949, 1952, 1954, the 1955 land) and the 1974 TV footage were not.
why.d: No communication to BP after 4 November 1974 is held yet. The judgment's own words (EG [1987] 2 EGLR 168, pp. 170–171) support the timing.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Her reply, or her 1974 solicitors' letters to BP Pension Trust, BP Properties or Linklaters & Paines (4 November 1974 to 26 March 1983); BP's list of documents in the 1984–86 action; the 1959 and 1965 offer files; the 1955 order and its plan.

argument.court: The letters made her BP's licensee from receipt unless she repudiated them; it 'may be' the result would have been different had she plainly rejected them, and the court found she instead followed advice to do nothing until 11 December 1974.
argument.ours: Her answer to permission was always no. The letters asked for no reply, reached her solicitor on the morning of a court hearing, and the warrant was withdrawn before she could give instructions: BP 'neither sought nor waited for her acceptance'. Silence was not acceptance, and she wrote back.

steps.event: John Williams's tenancy surrendered; new yearly tenancy granted to Frederick Buckler (the 1939 plan shows Parcel B, not the house parcel)
Landlord's agents write that they do not propose to proceed with the letting
Further attempt to make Frederick a tenant (family archive)
Possession taken of all the farm except the farmhouse and garden; which land the order covered is unclear on the family's reading
Tenancy of the farmhouse and garden offered by Western Ground Rents
Tenancy offered again by Western Ground Rents' agents
steps.state: Never signed, no rent paid (family archive)

steps.event: BP Pension Trust's action adjourned part heard; her defence pleads title by adverse possession
Leave to enforce the 1962 order; warrant to issue but not be enforced until 31 October
Her solicitors appeal: she had 'no opportunity of presenting her case'; stay appointment fixed for 4 November
Licence letters dated; sent to her solicitor, not to her; neither asks for a reply
Solicitor receives the letters that morning; BP does not attend; judge stays execution 'pending Mrs Buckler's agreement'; solicitor phones her for instructions
steps.state: Her answer awaited by the court

steps.event: BP's solicitors withdraw the warrant 'before she had given any instructions'
Her written reply to the letters (family record)
Court of Appeal: no repudiation, so licensee from receipt

Later courts: the letters came 'out of the blue' (Smith v Molyneaux [2016] UKPC 35 para 28); Buckler is not authority that a unilateral licence ends adverse possession in every case, and the rejection question was left open (Brown v Ridley [2024] UKUT 14 (LC) para 155)

rows.title: The 1939 agreement: John Williams's signature against his real signature on family heirlooms
rows.what: A May 1939 agreement by which Western Ground Rents let 5.30 acres of pasture to John Williams the younger, then 72, signed before a bank cashier. The family holds heirlooms carrying his own signature, and the signature on the agreement does not match them. In our framework this letting is where the 'permissive from this date' paper trail begins: the 1949 re-grant, the 1952 withdrawal, the 1955 possession order and, through its ambiguity, the 1962 order the 1987 court relied on.

why.a: A visible mismatch is a strong indicator, but forgery is shown only by an examiner's comparison.
why.b: The judgment rests on the 1949 surrender and re-grant and the 1962 order, not the 1939 letting itself; the link runs through that chain.
why.c: The heirloom signatures and the agreement were not compared in 1987.
why.d: Dated specimens are held on the heirlooms; the agreement is seen only in an angled photograph, and no examiner has compared them.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Photograph the heirloom signatures with dates and provenance; copy page 1 of the agreement at Glamorgan Archives (DBDT123/7); a forensic document examiner's comparison. A finding that he did not sign would lift limbs 1 and 4.
rows.status: Open: heirloom specimens held; comparison to arrange
rows.score_note: Rescored 14 Nov 2026 (owner: heirloom specimens held). Previous 20.

rows.title: The 12-year paper playbook: registrations without root title, never disclosed to the occupiers
rows.what: Our working framework: while the family's occupation was cast in court as permissive or adverse, the companies themselves used the 12-years-uncontested route on paper, registering land as proprietors without a root title and without telling the family: the woodland (1961 deed, first registered 1982), the green (VG41, 1970) and the farmhouse (1982–83). The 1987 court held that Western Ground Rents' agents walking the land from time to time was not possession, which on our reading is why the company could not take the farmhouse that way and conveyed in 1969.

why.a: Each registration is on record; no document yet shows a declaration that misstated the occupiers' position.
why.b: The 1987 court did not rely on these registrations; the pattern bears on how the 1962 order and the 1983 title came to be.
why.c: The pattern across all the dated events (the twelve-year chart) was never put to any court.
why.d: Registers and recitals only; the applications and declarations behind them are unread.

rows.what_would_raise_it: The first-registration applications and statutory declarations for WA735527, VG41 and WA240304, showing what each said about occupation and the family's ownership plea.
rows.status: Open: framework lead (Mr Wolf seed score)

rows.title: July 1955: possession taken beyond the order, and the 1962 order built on its ambiguity
rows.what: Our case: the 1955 order was executed beyond the land it covered, taking the woodland north and the green south of the house, while the farmhouse and garden were left out. The 1962 order on the farmhouse rested on reading that ambiguity one way, and it was the 1962 order that BP enforced in 1974.

why.a: Neither the order nor the officer's return has been located, so nothing yet shows a knowing over-reach.
why.b: The judgment records possession taken in 1955 of all parts of the farm except the farmhouse and garden, and the 1987 appeal concerned only the farmhouse and garden.
why.c: Catalogue placeholders only; both documents are still being traced.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Trace the 1955 order and the sheriff's or bailiff's return (High Court and sheriff records), then overlay them on the boundary plans. To bear on 1987 it would also have to touch the farmhouse plot.
rows.status: Open: records not located (Mr Wolf seed score)

rows.title: 1982–83 first registration of the farmhouse without the occupier
rows.what: The farmhouse was registered separately (title WA240304, application on Form 1C, register edition 23 February 1983) while BP's own 1974 action against the occupier, Mary (Nancy) Williams, had never been finally heard.

why.a: HM Land Registry's file lists the Form 1C application and a letter of 8 April 1983. What the declaration stated about occupation has not been read.
why.b: The Court of Appeal held that any title she had acquired would have been an overriding interest binding the registration, so the registration date was not why she lost.
why.c: HM Land Registry's 2026 schedule and complaint replies are new.
why.d: An official anomaly; the declaration itself is unread.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Read WA240304 item 11 (Form 1C with its statutory declaration) and item 7 (the 8 April 1983 letter), already requested from HM Land Registry. A declaration that misstated occupation would lift limbs 1 and 4.
rows.status: Open: HM Land Registry request pending

rows.title: 2 February 1987: the two titles merged while the appeal was pending
rows.what: HM Land Registry merged the farmhouse title (WA240304) into the main title (WA231076) on 2 February 1987, while the appeal was before the Court of Appeal.

why.a: Who applied, and why at that moment, is unread.
why.b: The court's description of the registration matches the register as merged, but it held the registration date was not why the occupier lost.
why.c: The amalgamation application and plan are listed on HM Land Registry's file (WA231076 item 14).

rows.what_would_raise_it: Obtain WA231076 item 14: the application, its plan, the title extents before and after, and any correspondence about the pending appeal.
rows.status: Open: record requested (Mr Wolf seed score)

rows.title: 1974 TV footage of Mary (Nancy) Williams, never before the 1987 court
rows.what: Two pieces of 1974 television footage show her on camera, including HTV Report Wales of 1 November 1974, 'Protest at a Cottage In Llandough Over Eviction Plans', three days before her solicitor received the licence letters. The 1987 court found she was 'not asserting' any claim to ownership after the letters; footage of her protesting the eviction in the same week bears directly on that finding.

why.a: Nothing yet shows BP knew of the footage and kept it back.
why.b: Goes to the court's finding that she asserted no claim to ownership around the letters.
why.d: Located but not yet viewed in full or catalogued with archive references.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Archive copies with references and broadcast dates, a transcript of what she said, and anything showing BP or its solicitors knew of the coverage.
rows.status: Open: footage located (Mr Wolf seed score)

rows.title: 1877 Bute–Thomas agreement and the 1928 last rent
rows.what: Our case: the farmhouse plot left the Bute estate under an 1877 arrangement with Daniel Thomas & Son, with rent ending in 1928. If so, the farmhouse lay outside the 1916 and 1949 tenancies and the 1938 conveyance, and the paper title the court relied on would fail for it.

why.a: Nothing yet points to anyone knowingly hiding it.
why.b: The court started from BP's 'paper title to the farm' and a 1916 tenancy of 'the whole of the farm'.
why.c: The 1938 conveyance and plan are not located; the family copy has no scan.
why.d: The 1877 agreement, plan and 1928 receipt are unread originals.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Produce the 1877 agreement with its plan and the 1928 receipt, and locate the 25 December 1938 conveyance (Bute and Mountjoy Ltd to Western Ground Rents) with its plan.

rows.title: The 31 December 1969 conveyance and the 1971 abstract missing from the title files
rows.what: In September 1974 BP Pension Trust obtained leave to enforce the 1962 possession order 'as successors in title to Western Ground Rents'. The 1969 conveyance from Western Ground Rents is not among the documents lodged on either first-registration file.

why.a: No record yet of anyone knowing a deed was missing or misdescribed.
why.b: The court held that enforcement of the 1962 judgment 'was still open to the landlords at October 31 1974'. Only the judgment creditor or its successor could enforce it.
why.c: HM Land Registry's 2026 lists of first-registration documents leave out the 1969 deed, though both root deeds recite it.
why.d: Absence from a list of lodged documents does not prove the deed did not exist; the deed itself is unread.

rows.what_would_raise_it: The 1969 conveyance itself (requested from HM Land Registry and the BP Archive) and the 1974 affidavit for leave: check whether the benefit of the 1962 judgment was expressly passed on.

rows.title: 31 October 1974 licence letters: could BP Properties give a licence?
rows.what: The Court of Appeal answered the 'wrong company' point from the letters' own words that BP Properties Ltd 'had agreed to buy'. Completion came only in May 1975, and HM Land Registry's file adds a plan to that sale dated 23 February 1975.

why.a: No record yet shows the writers knew the 'agreed to buy' words were untrue.
why.b: The whole result rests on the licence of BP Properties Ltd: 'from the time of her receipt of the letters, Mrs Buckler was in possession ... by the licence of BP Properties Ltd'.
why.c: The February 1975 plan is new, but the court already knew completion was in May 1975.
why.d: Catalogue entries only; the conveyance and any recital of the contract date are unread.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Read the 23 May 1975 conveyance (WA240304 item 12) and its plan for the date of the contract for sale. A contract dated after 31 October 1974 would lift limbs 1 and 3.

rows.title: 1975 conveyance reservations and 'safeguard your future occupation'
rows.what: The 1974 letters gave the sale to BP Properties as 'the only way' to 'safeguard your future occupation'. The 23 May 1975 conveyance, as entered on the register, kept development rights over the farmhouse plot.

why.a: Several documented facts: the letters' stated purpose, beside the reservations the register records from the 1975 conveyance.
why.b: The court decided the letters' legal effect; the writer's motive played no part in that reasoning.
why.c: New to the record, but the deed was most likely in the 1986 trial bundle.
why.d: A register view, not an official copy; the deed is unread.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Read the 1975 conveyance with its plan: whether the 'Retained Land' is the rest of the farm, and the contract date.

rows.title: Title papers taken from the blanket box (1950)
rows.what: The judgment records that documents proving title were 'never produced'. A typed statement from about 1974 records that in June 1950 a Penarth estate agent had the family's papers taken from a blanket box.

why.a: Second-hand: what a lodger told her the agent asked him to do. Nothing yet links the agent to Western Ground Rents or BP.
why.b: The missing papers appear only in the judgment's background; the decision turned on the 1974 letters.
why.c: The statement was with the family from 1974; no record shows it went before the 1986 trial.
why.d: An unsigned, undated typed copy with its last page missing.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Anything tying the Penarth agent to Western Ground Rents, the Bute estate office or their agents about 1949–55 (directories, probate, agency records).

rows.title: The 29 March 1961 woodland deed
rows.what: A deed between Western Ground Rents, South Western Brick & Tile and Cardiff City Corporation, known only from its recital on the woodland title WA735527.

why.a: Gap only: dealing over ground next to the occupied farm without reference to the occupier.
why.b: The 1987 judgment does not rely on it, and the appeal concerned only the farmhouse and garden.
why.c: Known only by recital; never inspected.
why.d: No copy, image or transcript held.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Order the deed and its plan recited on WA735527 and overlay the plan on the farm boundary.
rows.status: Open: deed orderable (Mr Wolf seed score)

rows.title: Village green VG41 (1970)
rows.what: Land was registered as village green VG41 in 1970 by Glamorgan County Council, whose own planning committee had heard Mary (Nancy) Williams object in 1958 that family land had been 'wrongfully appropriated'.

why.a: No VG41 application has been read, and the 1965 Act let an authority register a green without one, so no false declaration is shown.
why.b: The judgment does not mention the green, so it cannot have caused the 1987 decision. A separate route (correcting the register), not a reopening ground.
why.c: The 1958 Western Mail report is new to the record.
why.d: A newspaper report of her words; the VG41 file is unread.

rows.what_would_raise_it: The VG41 register sheet, the 1970 application or the authority's own-motion minute, and any objection (already asked of the Vale of Glamorgan).

rows.title: Missing public records and 'no records found' answers
rows.what: The 1988 demolition, Cadw's missing 1988 file and answers that records 'would have been destroyed'. Limitation Act 1980 s.32 postpones time where facts were deliberately concealed.

why.a: Cadw gave two explanations for the lost file.
why.b: All of this happened after the July 1987 judgment, so it cannot have caused it.
why.d: Not yet assessable: no destruction log has been read.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Destruction logs and retention schedules showing when and why files were removed (asked for). Only a record of deliberate removal would count, not a modern search that found nothing.
rows.status: Parked as a reopening ground: after 1987

rows.title: The 1988 footage: held by The National Archives, released a month after the 2025 concerns
rows.what: ITV footage of the 1988 demolition period was acquired by The National Archives (about 2012 on our understanding) and released on 25 July 2025, about a month after the family first raised concerns of concealment in June 2025. Whether it ever aired is unknown.

why.a: The release timing is on record; nothing yet shows the footage was held back deliberately.
why.b: It postdates the July 1987 judgment, so it cannot have caused it; it bears on concealment after the event.
why.d: Accession and release records are not yet held.

rows.what_would_raise_it: The National Archives' accession date, access decisions and any closure review for the footage; broadcast logs showing whether it aired.
rows.status: Open: records to request (Mr Wolf seed score)

rows.title: Letters addressed to 'Mrs Buckler'
rows.what: The 1974 letters were addressed to 'Mrs Buckler', not Mary (Nancy) Williams.

why.a: None: a different name is not dishonesty.
why.c: Not fresh: the court knew both names.

rows.title: Burials under the farmhouse plot known before 1987?
rows.what: Was knowledge of the burials found under the farm (1,026 recorded in 1994) held before the 1986–87 trial and kept from the court?

why.a: No record of anyone knowing of burials under the plot before 1990.
why.b: What lay underground has no bearing on whether the 1974 letters turned possession into permission.
why.c: The 1990 and 2005 archaeology reports are new, but neither shows knowledge before 1987.
why.d: Credible sources, but they would not have influenced the decision.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Only a document dated before July 1987 showing that BP, its agents or the archaeologists knew of burials under the farmhouse plot.

priority_note: Our case: the order of importance in the family's working framework (permission never accepted; the 1939 signature; the 12-year paper playbook; the 1955 and 1962 orders). Threshold score: the rubric order. The gauges always use the threshold score.
